In this lesson you will learn about the Schmitt Trigger.
INTRODUCTIONM
A Schmitt Trigger converts an input waveform of any shape and amplitude into square wave pulses of constant amplitude.
Because of this function, Schmitt triggers are often called Squaring Amplifiers or Level Detectors.
The "clean" output can be used as the input to other circuits that would not have accepted the irregular input.

Each pulse is of the same duration (5 time intervals). At T1, the input is zero and the output is zero. This is the static condition of the circuit.
At T2, the input begins to increase in amplitude. However, the output remains at zero.
At T3, the input reaches the upper threshold level of the Schmitt trigger and the output immediately goes high.
For this particular Schmitt trigger, the upper threshold level is 2.5 volts.
As long as the input remains above 2.5 V, the output will continue to be high.
At T4, the input drops below the upper threshold level. This causes the output to immediately drop to zero.
If the input signal remains below 2.5 V the output continues to be zero.
No matter what the shape of the input signal, the output is high anytime the input exceeds the threshold.
The output is low anytime the input signal is below the threshold.
This simple block diagram illustrates the operation of a Schmitt trigger.
The voltage divider determines the upper threshold level of the circuit.
Once the threshold is reached, Q1 starts to become saturated (zero output). This begins to place Q2 in cutoff (high output).
As Q2 begins to reach cutoff, feedback from Q2 drives Q1 deeper into saturation which places Q2 further towards cutoff.
This process happens incredibly fast. As a result, the output of Q2 goes high immediately when the upper threshold level is reached.
This is an actual Schmitt Trigger circuit. Notice the voltage divider at the input..
In the static condition (no input), Q1 is OFF. This allows Vcc to forward bias Q2.
When Q2 is forward biased, a voltage divider is formed by R6 and R8. About .26 volts is dropped across R6. This produces a low output from the circuit.
The .26 volts (a small positive bias) is present on the emitter of Q1.
When the input exceeds the threshold, Q1 begins to conduct. The voltage on the collector decreases to a level insufficient to forward bias Q2.
Since Q2 is at cutoff, the output is Vcc.
With Q2 OFF, the voltage divider of (R6 and R8) for all practical purposes, no longer exists. The voltage that was present across R6, when Q2 was ON, has been substantially reduced.
Without the small positive bias contributed by R6 to the emitter of Q1, Q1 conducts harder.
The harder Q1 conducts, the more Q2 is driven to cutoff. The more Q2 is driven to cutoff, the harder Q1 conducts.
Feedback is the key to Schmitt Trigger operation. It assures very short rise and fall times of the output..
RISE AND FALL TIMES - Rise and fall time is the time interval between the 10% point and the 90% point on the edge of a pulse.
